name: Flyovers and grade separation (layers, ramps, merges and diverges in the network graph and in vehicle behaviour)
type: model (network representation of grade separation plus merge/diverge behaviour model, with Indian geometric standards)
maintainer: Network representation: Eclipse SUMO / netconvert (DLR), A/B Street and osm2streets (Dustin Carlino and contributors), ASAM OpenDRIVE (ASAM e.V.), OpenStreetMap community (layer/bridge/link tagging). Behaviour: MOBIL and traffic-simulation.de (Treiber, Kesting, Helbing). Indian geometry: Indian Roads Congress (IRC:92-2017 Guidelines for the Design of Interchanges in Urban Areas)
first_release: MOBIL published 2007; IRC:92 first edition 1985, revised 2017; OpenDRIVE first public release 2006 [uncertain]; osm2streets split out of A/B Street about 2022 [uncertain]
last_activity: Checked 2026-11-11: osm2streets last commit 2 Oct 2025 (shallow clone); SUMO netconvert docs current; ASAM OpenDRIVE 1.8.0 specification online; traffic-simulation.de repo active; IRC:92-2017 current edition
licence: SUMO EPL-2.0; osm2streets / A/B Street Apache-2.0; traffic-simulation.de GPL-3.0; OSM data ODbL; ASAM OpenDRIVE specification under ASAM terms (free to read online) [uncertain]; IRC codes copyrighted
language: SUMO/netconvert C++; osm2streets Rust (with osm2streets-js WASM bindings); traffic-simulation.de JavaScript; OpenDRIVE is an XML format
code_availability: Source: github.com/eclipse-sumo/sumo, github.com/a-b-street/osm2streets (layer field in osm2streets/src/road.rs), github.com/movsim/traffic-simulation-de (onramp.html, offramp.html, mergeDiverge in js/road.js). OpenDRIVE: specification only. IRC:92-2017: PDF on law.resource.org
maintenance_health: SUMO actively maintained; its z-coordinate/elevation support from OSM is labelled experimental. osm2streets maintained at lower cadence (last commit October 2025); a TODO in block.rs notes block tracing is 'Incorrect near bridges/tunnels'. traffic-simulation.de ramp scenarios are stable and long-lived
scale: Microscopic (merge/diverge lane-change behaviour); network representation is scale-independent
car_following: Merges reuse the car-following model: in traffic-simulation.de the on-ramp ends in a standing virtual obstacle so ramp vehicles brake with IDM if they find no gap; merging vehicles are inserted into the main road and the IDM handles the follower's response. In SUMO, lanes ending at a zipper junction produce slow-down only on demand based on neighbours
lane_model: MOBIL (traffic-simulation.de): safety criterion acc'(B') > -b_safe; incentive acc'(M') - acc(M) > p[acc(B') - acc'(B')] + a_thr (the acc(B) term is dropped in the implementation), defaults a_thr = 0.2 m/s2, a_bias = 0.2 m/s2, b_safe = 4 m/s2 (below the about 9 m/s2 physical maximum), politeness p 0 to 0.5. Mandatory lane change at on-ramps: a large bias toward the target lane plus the safety criterion only; setLCMandatory marks mandatory zones on on-ramps and before lane drops; b_safe grows aggressive in congestion because it is speed-dependent. Off-ramps: each road stores off-ramp position and side; vehicles whose route continues on the ramp get a strong lane-change bias toward the exit as they approach, and mergeDiverge moves them onto the ramp along the parallel section. Merges happen over a parallel section of length L with the upstream link as master. SUMO: lanes end at junctions; acceleration lanes can be added by --ramps.guess; strategic lane changes (LC2013 model) start early enough to reach the exit lane; lane drops can be junction type zipper
lateral_model_type: None in the reference ramp models (lane-based MOBIL). For Indian traffic the merge zone should reuse our strip-based lateral model: a ramp is an extra set of strips that ends, so ramp vehicles must move laterally into main-road strips before the nose
junction_model: Grade separation means there is no junction where a flyover crosses the road below; interactions happen only at ramp merge/diverge nodes and at the at-grade junction under the flyover (handled by the B06 junction model). Merge nodes behave as priority junctions (main road major, ramp minor) or zipper merges
signal_control_modes: N/A for the flyover itself (uninterrupted). The at-grade junction underneath is usually signalised; see B06
flyover_support: SUMO: yes. Crossings without shared nodes create no junction, so overpasses work topologically; z data only affects 3D/visualisation and slope; ramps are ordinary edges, with optional acceleration lanes from --ramps.guess (disabled by default; ramp-length 100 m; edges slower than ramps.min-highway-speed = 21.94 m/s, about 79 km/h, are not treated as highways). osm2streets/A/B Street: yes topologically (OSM shared nodes), with an integer layer per road for drawing order. traffic-simulation.de: on-ramp, off-ramp and lane-closing scenarios built from road objects with merge/diverge connections; no explicit layering, roads may overlap visually. OpenDRIVE: yes, roads without a junction element simply cross; each road carries an elevationProfile (cubic polynomials in s) and a lateralProfile (superelevation, shape)
grade_separation_handling: OSM: a flyover is tagged bridge=yes plus layer=1 (layer values usually -5..5, default 0, not tagged at ground level); ways at different layers must NOT share a node where they cross, because a shared node destroys the vertical order and creates a false junction; ramps are highway=*_link (e.g. primary_link, trunk_link) and connect via shared nodes at the ramp ends; validators (JOSM) flag crossing ways without layer differences. SUMO netconvert: --osm.layer-elevation H reconstructs relative z by raising each layer by H metres, limited by --osm.layer-elevation.max-grade (default 10% at 50 km/h, scaled with speed); --osm.elevation imports ele tags (experimental); --junctions.join (recommended for OSM, join-dist 10 m) merges clustered nodes; --junctions.join-same (disabled by default) would join unconnected nodes at similar coordinates and must stay off for flyovers [uncertain about failure frequency]. osm2streets: Road.layer parsed from the OSM layer tag (non-integer values warned), exported as a render property for roads and lane markings, and collapse_intersections refuses to merge two roads whose layers differ; topology comes only from shared OSM nodes. OpenDRIVE: grade separation is implicit (no junction record) and z comes from elevationProfile, so a tool must compute heights to draw overpasses. Repair checks we should implement for user-drawn or imported networks: (1) two links crossing in plan view on the same level without a shared node is an error to flag; (2) a node shared by links of different levels is only allowed where a ramp lands; (3) ramp grades checked against 4% desirable / 6% maximum (IRC:92)
vehicle_types: Ramps and flyovers carry the same classes as the arterial; IRC:92 notes NMT facilities should be provided under the flyover (dedicated or shared), implying cycles and pedestrians use the at-grade road. Some Indian flyovers prohibit slow vehicles or two-wheelers by local order [uncertain]. Heavy vehicles slow down on 4-6% ramps; whether to model grade effects on acceleration is optional
gridlock_policy: Merge deadlocks occur when the ramp end is blocked: in traffic-simulation.de ramp vehicles simply wait at the virtual obstacle at the end of the merge section (no teleport), which can spill back onto the at-grade road. SUMO would eventually teleport vehicles stuck at the ramp end (time-to-teleport) [uncertain default]. Our build: no teleport; let spillback propagate and report it, because spillback from flyover ramps into the junction underneath is exactly what users want to see
mixed_traffic_support: Reference ramp models are lane-based and homogeneous. In India, two-wheelers squeeze into gaps at the merge nose and ramps often have no proper acceleration lane, so merging is closer to forced, zipper-like interleaving than MOBIL gap acceptance [uncertain: qualitative]
non_lane_behaviour: Indian arterials are typically median-divided with three to four lanes per direction, connected to the junction by two- to four-lane ramps (Maji et al. 2015); traffic below the flyover is non-lane-based and often unmanaged. A strip-based model handles the merge as lateral movement into free strips with a minimum lateral clearance per class, with smaller acceptable longitudinal gaps for 2W
seepage_filtering_support: Not applicable to ramps directly. At the at-grade junction beneath the flyover, seepage at the stop line applies as for any signal (see the seepage item)
per_class_parameters: No published Indian per-class merge or ramp gap-acceptance values were found [uncertain]. Use MOBIL defaults (a_thr 0.2 m/s2, b_safe 4 m/s2) with class-specific safe deceleration and the B06 critical gaps as merge-time gaps
indian_calibration_evidence: Maji, Maurya, Nama and Sahu (Journal of Modern Transportation 2015) used microsimulation to compare intersection layouts under a flyover for heterogeneous traffic and report that detailed geometric design guidelines for weak-lane-discipline traffic do not exist. A Bengaluru integrated traffic microsimulation report (Hebbal area) studied a corridor with four lanes and four up/down ramps and compared 2-lane versus 4-lane bidirectional flyover options on Sankey Road [uncertain: tool and calibration details not checked]
calibration_dataset_used: Not open: project-specific counts for the Bengaluru microsimulation report; field data for the Maji et al. study. No open Indian on-ramp trajectory dataset found [uncertain]
calibration_method: Not reported in the sources checked [uncertain]
validation_against_field_case: Bengaluru Hebbal/Sankey Road flyover options (microsimulation report on data.opencity.in) [uncertain]; Pune flyover at Karmaveer Vithalrao Yadav Chowk, 13.25 m overall width for four lanes (TCE project page)
reuse_mode: Use as data and port the model: adopt OSM conventions (bridge + layer, *_link) and osm2streets' integer layer per road if importing; port the traffic-simulation.de mergeDiverge pattern (parallel merge section, virtual obstacle at the end, route-driven exit bias) and MOBIL mandatory lane change into our strip model; take ramp geometry defaults from IRC:92-2017. No code reuse needed
effort_within_72_hours: About 6-8 hours. 1 h: add a level (integer) and optional z-profile to links; render higher levels after lower ones with a shadow/outline, and hit-test highest level first. 1-2 h: editor tool 'flyover over junction' that creates a level-1 link chain over an existing node plus four ramps (up/down per direction) landing 150-300 m from the node [uncertain distance], and service roads remain at level 0. 2-3 h: merge zone (ramp strips end; lateral move with safety check; virtual obstacle at nose) and diverge zone (route-aware bias starting about 300 m upstream; deceleration length 90-120 m). 1 h: validation checks (same-level crossings without nodes, grades). Cut: true 3D, elevation-based acceleration, cloverleaf/directional interchanges, OpenDRIVE import
licence_constraint: No code is copied, so no constraint. If osm2streets (Apache-2.0) is used for OSM import, keep its notice; OSM-derived networks must carry ODbL attribution; do not copy traffic-simulation.de JS (GPL-3.0)
known_limitations: OSM layer is relative and local, not an elevation; netconvert's layer-to-elevation is a heuristic that may need manual correction, and z support is experimental. SUMO --ramps.guess will not detect Indian urban flyover ramps because their speeds are below the 79 km/h highway threshold; ramps must be set explicitly (--ramps.set). osm2streets uses layer mainly for rendering and intersection collapsing; its block tracing is known to be incorrect near bridges/tunnels. traffic-simulation.de roads have no layering and its updates are parallel without sequencing inter-road dependencies. MOBIL is lane-based and assumes a lane to merge into. IRC:92 is written for interchanges and gives few flyover-specific cross-section values; typical Indian urban flyovers are 2 lanes per direction (about 7.0-7.5 m per carriageway) or 2-lane bidirectional, with the at-grade junction and service roads below [uncertain: generalisation from examples]
documented_failures: Joining nodes at a crossing (shared node between a bridge and the road below) creates a phantom at-grade junction; the OSM wiki explicitly warns this destroys vertical order. Renderers that sort by a single pass of layer draw overpasses under highways (OSM Community 2025 Shortbread vector-tile report). Indian flyovers often move the bottleneck to the unmanaged junction underneath and to the ramp landing points (Maji et al. 2015). IRC:92 identifies rear-end crashes at entrances as the most frequent interchange crash type, caused by short acceleration lanes
validation_approach: IRC:92 is a design standard (no simulation validation). Maji et al. compared layouts by microsimulated operational performance. traffic-simulation.de demonstrates on-ramp breakdown and capacity drop qualitatively. For our build: test that two crossing links on different levels never interact; that ramp merge capacity drops when main-road flow rises; that a blocked ramp spills back to the at-grade junction; and that a flyover diverts through traffic so the junction underneath shows lower delay
takeaway_for_our_build: 1) Grade separation is a topology rule, not geometry: vehicles interact only through shared nodes and conflict points computed per node; never infer junctions from plan-view crossings. Store level (int) per link for rendering and validation only. 2) Spatial queries must be link-local (or include level), because a world-space grid would make vehicles on a flyover see vehicles on the road beneath (link to D02). 3) Provide a one-click 'flyover over junction' template using IRC:92-2017 defaults: 2 lanes (7.0-7.5 m) per direction, ramp grade 4% (max 6%), urban design speed 80 km/h main / 40-50 km/h ramp, acceleration lane 180-250 m, deceleration lane 90-120 m, vertical clearance 5.5 m, ramp capacity per IRC Table 6.3 (two-lane 7.0 m: 2400 PCU/h; 4-lane divided 7.5 m: 2700 PCU/h/direction). 4) Merge = ramp strips end at a nose with a virtual obstacle; vehicles move laterally into free main-road strips if the new follower's required braking stays below b_safe (4 m/s2, lower for heavy vehicles) and after a waiting time accept smaller gaps (forced merge). 5) Diverge = route-aware bias starting about 300 m upstream so exiting vehicles move toward the exit side. 6) Keep service roads and the at-grade junction underneath as normal level-0 links so users see that the flyover shifts congestion to ramp landings and the junction below
